references.text: Israel was God's treasured possession, his 'own' among all peoples. When John writes that 'he came to his own,' it points back to God's covenant relationship with Israel as his special possession ([ref:2 Mos 19:5-6|Exodus 19:5-6]).

Israel is described as a holy people, chosen by the Lord as his treasured possession above all other peoples on earth. This is the background for why Jesus came to 'his own' ([ref:5 Mos 7:6|Deuteronomy 7:6]).
Isaiah laments that Israel does not know their Lord—the ox knows its owner, but Israel does not know. This parallels how Jesus's own people did not receive him ([ref:Jes 1:3|Isaiah 1:3]).

The prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant tells of how he was despised and forsaken by people—no one esteemed him. This foretold the rejection that John describes: 'his own did not receive him' ([ref:Jes 53:1-3|Isaiah 53:1-3]).

The Lord sent his servants, the prophets, again and again to Israel, but they would not listen or learn. This repeated rejection of God's messengers parallels how the people of Israel did not receive Christ ([ref:Jer 7:25-26|Jeremiah 7:25-26]).

The parable of the wicked tenants describes how God's people repeatedly rejected his servants and finally his own Son—an illustration of what John says about his own not receiving him ([ref:Matt 21:33-39|Matthew 21:33-39]).
Jesus weeps over Jerusalem because he wanted to gather her children, but they would not. This is a concrete unfolding of the rejection described in John 1:11 ([ref:Matt 23:37|Matthew 23:37]).

In the parable of the minas, the citizens say: 'We do not want this man to rule over us.' This directly mirrors the rejection in John 1:11, where his own did not receive him ([ref:Luk 19:14|Luke 19:14]).

Right after mentioning the rejection, John writes about those who nevertheless received him and were given the right to become children of God. The verse forms a contrast to the rejection in verse 11 ([ref:Joh 1:12-13|John 1:12-13]).

Jesus says that he has come in his Father's name, and they do not receive him; but if another comes in his own name, they will receive him. A direct confirmation of the theme in John 1:11 ([ref:Joh 5:43|John 5:43]).
Peter explains that God first sent his servant to the children of Israel—'his own'—to bless them. This confirms that the gospel came first to Jesus's own people ([ref:Apg 3:23-26|Acts 3:23-26]).

Paul and Barnabas say that God's word had to be spoken to the Jews first, but since they rejected it, they turn to the Gentiles. This reflects the rejection described in John 1:11 ([ref:Apg 13:46|Acts 13:46]).

Paul grieves over his fellow countrymen, the Israelites, who have received adoption, glory, covenants, and promises—and yet did not receive the Messiah. They were 'his own' who rejected him ([ref:Rom 9:4-5|Romans 9:4-5]).

Paul emphasizes that God has not rejected his people, even though a large majority rejected Christ. Israel's rejection is not God's final word—an important nuance to John 1:11 ([ref:Rom 11:1-2|Romans 11:1-2]).
